---
title: How fields interact
description: "Context forms at two scales: fields within one event, then events across the history."
engine: markdown
---

Consider the dispute-prediction example from
[Add transaction history](../learn/add-transaction-history.qmd). Each
observation contains a transaction history available at one account-review
cutoff, with the latest payment last. The model can use an amount together
with its merchant and the account's other transactions when predicting each
retained transaction's later dispute label.

RelFlow builds that context at two scales: fields belonging to one event
record, then events belonging to the same history. This keeps the relationship
between an amount and its merchant available when the model compares
transactions.

Field types define how visible values are encoded. Training learns how their
representations combine to support the configured objectives.
Each visible field occurrence becomes a numeric vector, or **embedding**. The
vectors processed by attention are called **tokens**. A transaction
**coordinate** is one position in the `trxns` list. Attention learns how each token's
representation should use information from other visible tokens.

```{typst}
//| label: fig-field-interactions
//| fig-cap: "Fields first interact within each transaction. Sequence attention then mixes all present tokens across the history; the column frame shows one possible comparison. Reduction decides what reaches the root."
//| fig-alt: "A grid of tokens with one row per transaction on May 21, May 27, and May 28 and one column per field: booked_at, amount, and merchant. The first row is framed as coordinate attention among the fields of one transaction. The amount column highlights one example of a cross-record comparison; sequence attention can mix all present tokens in the grid. An arrow leads from the grid to a learned summary labeled reduction."
#tokens(
  ("booked_at", "amount", "merchant"),
  (
    (label: [May 21], values: ([Thu 10:00], [32.00], [Station Cafe])),
    (label: [May 27], values: ([Wed 18:15], [56.20], [North Market])),
    (label: [May 28, latest], values: ([Thu 14:30], [84.50], [North Market])),
  ),
  within: [1. Coordinate attention: the fields of one transaction],
  across: [2. One example of cross-record comparison],
  reduce: [3. Reduction: what reaches the root],
)
```

## Within one transaction

Each visible field first supplies an embedding at each transaction coordinate.
Coordinate attention groups the direct sibling fields at the same coordinate:
`booked_at`, `amount`, and `merchant` from the first transaction interact with
one another. The other transactions have their own groups. This step allows an
amount's representation to depend on the merchant attached to that amount.

`disputed=rf.Boolean(mask=True)` keeps every dispute label out of the inputs
and supervises every retained transaction; the labels are never evidence.

Two histories can have the same total spend and merchant counts while pairing
the larger purchase with different merchants. Keeping each transaction's
fields together preserves that distinction as evidence for learning.

The coordinate encoder mixes direct leaf fields and the summaries from
reduced child branches at the same record position. For example, a transaction's
amount can interact with its nested purchase summary before the transaction
history is summarized. A child with `reduction=None` does not join this
coordinate group. With fewer than two participating tokens there is no
coordinate interaction to perform. Setting branch attention to `None` also
disables this encoder.

## Across the history

After coordinate attention, the branch concatenates its children's tokens into
one sequence and applies its sequence encoder. Tokens from different history
positions and different fields can now interact; comparisons are not limited
to one field's column. Across a longer history, the model can learn
patterns such as repeated purchases at one merchant, changing amounts, or
activity concentrated in a short period. Whether these patterns help predict
a dispute must be checked on held-out payments.

These two stages answer different questions:

| Stage | Available context | Example relationship |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Coordinate attention | Direct fields and reduced child summaries at one record position | Which merchant received this amount? |
| Sequence attention | Present child tokens across the branch | How does this transaction compare with earlier ones? |
| Branch reduction | The branch's encoded transactions | Which context should reach the observation root? |

Reduction is a separate step, described in [Branch summaries](branch-summaries.qmd).
With the default reduction, `trxns` passes a learned summary to its parent.
That summary includes the earlier and latest transactions; the root has no
duplicate amount or merchant fields. The summary is trained for the model's
objectives; it is not a readable transaction ledger or a guaranteed calculation
of a business statistic.

## Presence and position

Padding represents an absent coordinate. The encoder excludes it from attention
and restores zero output at absent positions. A null value at a present
coordinate has its own field state; replacing it with zero changes what the
model observes. See [field states](../datatypes/index.qmd).

Rotary position information gives attention a signal about token positions.
`booked_at=rf.DateParts(dateparts=["day_of_month", "day_of_week", "hour_of_day"])`
supplies calendar cycles, not elapsed time. Input ordering still belongs to
the application, as [Prepare observations](../learn/prepare-observations.qmd)
describes; position information does not repair an incorrectly ordered
collection or prevent future information from entering the inputs.

Sequence attention can use the complete retained collection, because every
prediction in this example shares one review cutoff.

Encoder updates use residual attention and feed-forward blocks with RMSNorm and
tanh GELU. Attention normalizes each head's projected queries and keys before
applying rotary positions, so attention logits do not grow with projection scale.
Architecture options and collection limits belong in the
[model tree](model-tree.qmd) and [Branch reference](../datatypes/branch.qmd).
